theme: The seductress; Wisdom personified, the craftsman at God’s side
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 7:1-8:36. Chapter 7 is a vivid warning about a seductive woman, and chapter 8 is one of the great poems of the Bible, in which Wisdom herself speaks. Read chapter 8 slowly. It is the high point of the first nine chapters.
settingTheScene: These two chapters set the opposite voices in sharp contrast. In chapter 7, a young man without sense is drawn to a smooth-talking woman. In chapter 8, Wisdom speaks, calling to all who will listen. She reveals that she is older than creation and was with God as he made the world. This is among the passages most important for how the church has understood the relationship between wisdom and Christ.
observation: “Bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart” (7:3).
“And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart” (7:10).
“All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter” (7:22).
“Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death” (7:27).
“Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice?” (8:1).
“The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil” (8:13).
“The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old” (8:22).
“Then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always” (8:30).
interpretation:
Chapter 7 tells the story like a short film. A young man with no sense walks along the street at twilight, near the corner of her house. A woman meets him with flattery, religious language (“I had to offer sacrifices”), and an invitation. He follows “as an ox goes to the slaughter.” The chapter describes the way sin deceives: it comes with smooth talk, a good reason, and a sense of safety. And the end is death.

The warning is not simply a moral rule. It is meant to help the reader see what he is walking into. The young man’s problem was lack of sense, but also lack of caution. He was in the wrong place at the wrong time. “Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways.”

Then Wisdom speaks. She calls from the heights, at the crossroads, and at the gates. Unlike the seductress, she calls openly. She offers “noble things,” truth, and righteousness. Her fruit is better than gold. Kings reign by her. And she says, “Those who love me I love, and those who seek me diligently find me.”

The center of chapter 8 is verses 22 to 31. Wisdom says that the LORD possessed her at the beginning, before the earth. She was there when he set the heavens in place and marked out the foundations of the earth. “I was beside him, like a master workman.” Wisdom is not a mere abstraction. She is portrayed as a person, present with God and delighting in him, and in the human race. Christians have long read this passage in the light of the New Testament as a shadow of Christ, though it should be read carefully. In its own setting, Wisdom is a poetic personification of God’s wisdom. In the light of the whole Bible, it points to the Son through whom the world was made.

The chapter ends with a stark choice: “Whoever finds me finds life… but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death.”
connection: John 1:1-3 says that the Word was with God in the beginning, and all things were made through him. Colossians 1:15-17 says Christ is “the firstborn of all creation” and that all things were created through him. 1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Jesus said, “Come to me, all who labor” (Matthew 11:28), the call of Wisdom in the form of a Savior.
application:
Notice what voices speak to you with smooth words today. Do they lead to life?

Read 8:22-31 aloud as praise to Christ, the one through whom all things were made.

Ask God to help you hate evil, as verse 13 describes.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from ways that lead to death.
Thank him for Wisdom who calls aloud.
Thank Christ, who was with the Father in the beginning.
